conversation.content:
Hi there—thank you so much for making time today. I’m Dr. Maya Bennett, a perinatal mental-health clinician. My whole job is helping new mothers sort through the emotional ups and downs that can come after childbirth.  

Right now I’d like to do a quick screening using the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale—usually shortened to the EPDS. It’s a 10-question tool that looks at how you’ve been feeling emotionally over the past seven days. It’s not a test of your parenting or character; it’s simply a snapshot that helps us see if you might benefit from extra support and what kind would feel most helpful to you.  

Everything you share is confidential. If any question feels hard to answer, we can pause or rephrase—our goal is to keep you comfortable and safe. We’ll move through the 10 questions one by one; you can answer in your own words and I’ll jot the numbers down on my end.  

Ready to begin? Here’s the first question:

Over the past week, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt difficult?

Honestly… I can still laugh if something’s genuinely funny—like when the baby makes those little faces—but it feels kind of muted. I have to remind myself to chuckle, and the joy doesn’t last. It’s like the laugh fades almost right away and I’m back to feeling tired and a little flat.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

Yeah… I’ve been able to laugh, but it doesn’t come as easily as it used to. Sometimes I’ll smile or chuckle if my husband says something silly, but it feels kind of forced—like I’m going through the motions more than really feeling it.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

I still get little sparks of excitement—like when I think about taking the baby to see my parents this weekend—but they’re pretty short-lived. Most of the time I’m just focused on getting through the next feeding or the next diaper change, so the enjoyment feels kind of dulled.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Sometimes, yeah. Like yesterday the baby was extra fussy and I kept thinking maybe it’s because my milk isn’t “good enough” or I did something wrong. I know rationally that babies have off days, but the thought still pops in and I feel guilty, even if I don’t really have a reason.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

A few times this week I’ve caught myself suddenly worrying that the baby isn’t breathing when he’s napping—just running through those “what-if” thoughts in my head even though he’s fine. There’s no real reason for it; the worry just shows up and my heart races until I check on him.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Once or twice I’ve had that sudden rush of fear—like I’m walking down the stairs with the baby and picture myself tripping, or I’ll hear a siren and imagine something awful happening. It’s quick, but my chest gets tight and I have to stop and breathe for a minute before the feeling passes.
Things have been getting on top of me

Yeah, some days it feels like the to-do list just keeps growing faster than I can tick things off. Between the night feedings, laundry, and trying to grab a shower, I’ll hit late afternoon and feel like I’m trudging through mud—like I’m barely keeping my head above water.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Not exactly “unhappy,” more like wound-up. When I finally lie down, my brain won’t settle—kept replaying every little noise the baby made or thinking I should sterilize the bottles again. I probably lose an hour or more most nights before I drift off, even when the baby’s already asleep.
I have felt sad or miserable

I do feel that way some evenings—kind of heavy and tearful for no clear reason. It’s not all day, but it hits after the sun goes down and the house gets quiet. I’ll look at the baby sleeping and instead of feeling relieved I just feel… sad, like I’m missing something I can’t name.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

I haven’t actually cried much—maybe once this week. I teared up in the shower feeling overwhelmed, but I wiped it off pretty quick so my husband wouldn’t notice. So no, it hasn’t gotten to full crying spells.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No—never. I might feel tired or low, but I haven’t had any thoughts like that.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 17: Screening Note – Postpartum Depression/Anxiety Screen  
Date: [today]

Source: 10-item Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS) analogue interview

Symptoms/Concerns endorsed  
- Anhedonia: reduced ability to experience pleasure; laughter feels “forced”  
- Low/flat mood: evening heaviness, tearfulness without precipitant  
- Guilt/worthlessness: self-blame when infant fussy; questions milk quality  
- Anxiety: intrusive “what-if” thoughts re: infant safety, sudden chest-tightness/panic  
- Overwhelm: daily tasks “trudging through mud,” feels behind  
- Sleep disturbance: difficulty settling mind after night feeds, ≥1 h latency  
- No crying spells; denies self-harm ideation

Pattern  
Mood and anxiety symptoms present >2 wk, worse evenings, functionally impairing rest and task management. No safety concerns.

Screening significance  
Moderate depressive symptoms with comorbid anxiety; possible minor postpartum depressive or anxiety disorder. Continue formal assessment (EPDS score, clinical interview, psychosocial supports, medical rule-out).
